title: Working cases for comparing early avant-garde and later receptions of art
purpose: Gather documented cases as evidence for investigating changing attitudes toward the cultural importance of art, without treating famous incidents as a representative sample or equating every controversy with a riot.
guidingQuestion: Did the historical avant-garde and its opponents treat art as art, including its forms and boundaries, as more broadly consequential than comparable publics tend to do today?
interpretiveCaution: A striking reaction is evidence to examine, not proof that an era took art more seriously. Seriousness need not mean approval; contemporary controversies can also be consequential, and their stakes may overlap with early ones.

cases.event: Fauvist paintings at the Paris Salon d'Automne
cases.documentedReaction: Paintings using non-naturalistic color drew hostile attention; critic Louis Vauxcelles's 'wild beasts' label became the movement's name.
cases.issueAtStake: Whether color detached from imitation could count as serious painting.
cases.consequence: The derogatory label became the durable public name of a new artistic movement.
cases.interpretivePossibility: A formal decision about color became an explicit matter of public critical judgment.
cases.qualification: A critic's phrase and reports of scandal do not establish a uniform response among Salon visitors; the work also attracted supporters and collectors.

sources.title: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Fauvism
Centre Pompidou, Le fauvisme et ses influences

cases.event: Proposed display of Nude Descending a Staircase at the Salon des Indépendants, Paris
respondents: other Cubist artists on the organizing committee
cases.documentedReaction: Cubist colleagues objected to displaying Duchamp's painting; it was withdrawn from the 1912 Salon des Indépendants.
cases.issueAtStake: The limits of acceptable experimentation within an already experimental group.
cases.consequence: Duchamp's work was not shown there, before its later American notoriety.
cases.interpretivePossibility: The historical avant-garde had consequential internal boundaries, not merely a united opposition to conventional taste.
cases.qualification: This was a dispute among artists, not evidence of a general public's reaction.

sources.title: Centre Pompidou, Marcel Duchamp educational dossier

cases.documentedReaction: Press clippings and reader parodies mocked Cubist work, especially Duchamp's painting; the show also drew large crowds and recorded sales, including that painting.
cases.issueAtStake: Whether new pictorial forms deserved the name and status of art.
cases.consequence: Modern art became a widely reported cultural controversy and an object of collecting, not simply rejection.
cases.interpretivePossibility: Ridicule and commercial interest could coexist within the same reception event.
cases.qualification: The archived press is not a census of visitor opinion; organizers also actively cultivated publicity.

cases.event: Chicago presentation of the Armory Show
respondents: School of the Art Institute students
cases.documentedReaction: On the show's last day, art students staged a mock trial of Matisse and burned copies—not originals—of three paintings. Public lectures debating the exhibition filled the Art Institute's hall and had to be repeated.
cases.issueAtStake: Whether an established art institution should confer its space and authority on the new art.
cases.consequence: The dispute was staged on museum grounds, covered by the press, and argued in public lectures.
cases.interpretivePossibility: This is a particularly concrete case of a local art institution and its own students contesting aesthetic legitimacy.
cases.qualification: The protest was theatrical and did not express every visitor's view; the Art Institute's research describes the response as mixed.

sources.title: Art Institute of Chicago, The Finale

cases.documentedReaction: Audience disruption and a physical altercation ended the concert before its program was complete; Schönberg publicly objected that a ticket did not entitle its holder to disrupt a performance.
cases.issueAtStake: Whether experimental concert music and its performers deserved the protections of a serious concert setting.
cases.consequence: The concert stopped, and the disturbance became a public controversy.
cases.interpretivePossibility: A fight over new music also became a fight over how an audience may behave inside an authoritative cultural institution.
cases.qualification: This was conflict among ticketed concertgoers and organizers, not evidence of society-wide attitudes.

sources.title: Arnold Schönberg Center, 1913 interview after the concert

cases.event: Paris premiere of The Rite of Spring, 29 May
cases.documentedReaction: The premiere met loud, divided reactions; disruptions made the performance difficult to hear. Later tellings have made the evening emblematic of an artistic 'riot.'
cases.issueAtStake: Unfamiliar rhythms, choreography, and expectations of what ballet should be.
cases.consequence: The event became a durable story of modernist rupture, while the work went on to have a very different reception.
cases.interpretivePossibility: The conflict included defenders and opponents, making it a contest within an invested audience rather than undifferentiated hostility.
cases.qualification: The degree of physical violence in the familiar 'riot' story is disputed; recent press scholarship explicitly warns about myth-making and the select composition of the premiere audience.

sources.title: Library of Congress, All Publicity Is Good
Cambridge University Press, The Rite of Spring in the Parisian Press

cases.event: First public concert of Luigi Russolo's intonarumori, Milan
cases.documentedReaction: Accounts describe a crowd already hostile before the noise-instrument concert began and a confrontation between Futurist performers and people in the audience.
cases.issueAtStake: The proposal that mechanical and urban noises could become musical material.
cases.consequence: The disturbance became part of the Futurists' account of the event.
cases.interpretivePossibility: The performance deliberately courted confrontation, so reaction and artwork were partly intertwined.
cases.qualification: The most vivid accounts come from participants or partisan Futurist sources. Treat the scale and details of the confrontation as provisional until contemporary independent reporting is checked.

sources.title: MoMA, Russolo exhibition checklist

cases.event: Submission of Fountain to the Society of Independent Artists, New York
cases.documentedReaction: The organizers voted to reject the urinal despite the exhibition's no-jury policy. Duchamp resigned, and a defense appeared in The Blind Man.
cases.issueAtStake: Whether choosing and presenting an ordinary manufactured object could make it art.
cases.consequence: The object was excluded from that exhibition; its rejection became central to its later significance.
cases.interpretivePossibility: An institution designed to avoid gatekeeping still enforced a boundary around the category of art.
cases.qualification: Fountain was not displayed in the exhibition, so this is evidence of organizer and peer reaction, not a witnessed general-public scandal.

sources.title: Philadelphia Museum of Art, Marcel Duchamp and the Fountain Scandal

cases.event: U.S. customs classification and subsequent trial of Brancusi's Bird in Space
cases.documentedReaction: Customs officials declined to classify the abstract sculpture as tariff-exempt art. The resulting case was decided in Brancusi's favor in 1928.
cases.issueAtStake: Whether sculpture must imitate a recognizable natural object to count legally as art.
cases.consequence: The definition of art carried an immediate financial consequence and was argued in court.
cases.interpretivePossibility: Art's category boundary was institutionally consequential outside a gallery or critical review.
cases.qualification: This is a state classification dispute, not a direct measure of popular taste.

sources.title: MoMA, But Is It Art? Constantin Brancusi vs. the United States

cases.event: Paris screenings and suppression of Buñuel's L'Âge d'or
cases.documentedReaction: At the Studio 28 cinema in December 1930, organized protesters damaged the screen, furnishings, and an adjoining Surrealist exhibition. Police authorities then prohibited further screenings in Paris.
cases.issueAtStake: A Surrealist challenge to bourgeois and religious conventions, combining artistic form with explicit social and religious provocation.
cases.consequence: The film was removed from public exhibition in France for decades.
cases.interpretivePossibility: Early avant-garde scandal was not always about form alone; religious and political offense could already drive organized action and censorship.
cases.qualification: An organized political attack should not be treated as a spontaneous verdict from an ordinary film audience.

sources.title: La Cinémathèque française, restoration history of L'Âge d'or

cases.event: John Cage performs Water Walk on I've Got a Secret
cases.documentedReaction: The host introduced Cage seriously while the studio audience laughed at the list of unconventional instruments and moments of the performance.
cases.issueAtStake: Whether sounds made with everyday objects could be presented as music on mass television.
cases.consequence: The performance proceeded as television entertainment rather than being stopped by its audience.
cases.interpretivePossibility: A formally experimental act could be framed and absorbed by a popular-media format.
cases.qualification: A game-show audience and a 1913 ballet premiere are not matched populations; the program's entertainment framing helped shape the reaction.

sources.title: John Cage Trust, John Cage's Secret

cases.event: Public dispute over Richard Serra's Tilted Arc, Federal Plaza, New York
cases.documentedReaction: Complaints about obstruction and unwanted imposition led to a three-day hearing in 1985; a GSA-appointed panel voted to remove the sculpture, which was dismantled in 1989.
cases.issueAtStake: The relationship between site-specific artistic autonomy and everyday public use of space.
cases.consequence: The work was removed and the commissioning agency changed its public-art procedures.
cases.interpretivePossibility: Contemporary art can still have serious public consequences when it changes people's shared environment, even without blasphemous or representational content.
cases.qualification: This is not directly comparable to a voluntarily attended gallery exhibition or performance; it complicates a simple form-versus-content story.

sources.title: U.S. General Services Administration, Art in Architecture: Selected Artworks 1997–2008

cases.event: New York City dispute with Brooklyn Museum over Sensation
cases.documentedReaction: The mayor condemned Ofili's painting and sought to penalize the museum through its city subsidy and building lease. A federal court barred the city from doing so because of the exhibition's viewpoint.
cases.issueAtStake: Religious offense, public subsidy, and the autonomy of a cultural institution.
cases.consequence: The dispute produced litigation over municipal support, not merely critical disagreement.
cases.interpretivePossibility: Public conflict over art persisted, but the immediate target was religious symbolism and public institutional support.
cases.qualification: The court record establishes governmental action and its limits; it does not measure the views of all New Yorkers or museum visitors.

sources.title: Brooklyn Institute of Arts v. City of New York, 1999 federal court opinion

cases.event: Reaction to Dana Schutz's Open Casket at the Whitney Biennial
cases.documentedReaction: The painting's depiction of Emmett Till prompted criticism and protest across museum and media settings concerning who may represent Black suffering.
cases.issueAtStake: The ethics and politics of racial representation, not simply formal experiment.
cases.consequence: The work became a focal point of public and institutional debate.
cases.interpretivePossibility: Art remained consequential where it touched contested social identity and representation.
cases.qualification: The museum's own retrospective is a useful institutional witness, not a complete account of all participants' positions.

sources.title: Whitney Museum, Reflecting on the 2017 Biennial

cases.event: Banksy's Girl with Balloon partly shreds after a Sotheby's sale
cases.documentedReaction: The work partly passed through a hidden shredder after the hammer fell; Sotheby's and the buyer treated the result as a new artwork, and the buyer completed the purchase. The work later sold again at Sotheby's in 2021.
cases.issueAtStake: Whether an apparent attack on a sale would disrupt or enhance the artwork's market identity.
cases.consequence: The gesture was rapidly incorporated into authentication, display, publicity, and resale.
cases.interpretivePossibility: A deliberately disruptive artistic gesture can be absorbed as a market event instead of provoking institutional exclusion.
cases.qualification: Sotheby's is an interested participant in the account; this is a market case, not a representative measure of contemporary public response.
